chapter: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
title: Whether the musicians' union gets players full-time work
summary: Most union members do not live off music, so players take any gig; Bunn says he would be working if he were not sick.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, the best thing is, of course, if you can get enough work just to keep playing your music.

That's why I asked you about the union, you know, because some people would say that the musicians' union is probably, compared to other types of unions, you know, probably they do less to get people work, you know, compared to -- I mean, if you're an iron worker, I mean the union is making contracts, you know, all the time, and people are working a lot of the time, you know. But the musicians' union, like in Philadelphia, for example, only about less than a third of the people that belong to the union make a full time living as musicians. Less than a third.
A lot of people just keep their membership because -- I don't know, prestige or they're
sentimental, or something like that, you know. In the union.
They might have another profession altogether, you know.
Yeah. Some of them just say, 'Well, it's too slow for me to get a good job, you know, working making good money for my family.'
And they just take anything that comes up.
Just like these gigs. Now, I imagine right now, if I wasn't sick, I could have a gig. I'd be working all the time.
